title: Stockton & Darlington: A Railway for the Public
summary: In 1825 a puffing engine called Locomotion pulled a long, wobbly train full of coal and cheering people across the north of England. It was the first public railway to use steam engines. Thousands of people lined the track to watch, and the price of coal dropped so much that ordinary families could keep warmer.

sections.heading: Coal Trapped Inland
paragraphs: In the early 1800s, south-west County Durham was sitting on a treasure. Around places like Witton Park, Etherley and West Auckland there were rich seams of coal. The trouble was getting it out to the world. The nearest good place to load coal onto ships was Stockton, on the River Tees, more than 20 miles away. From there, ships could carry it down the coast to London and other big markets. But between the pits and the river lay hills, farmland and rough roads, and moving coal by horse and cart was painfully slow and expensive. By the time a cartload reached Stockton, the cost of the journey had made the coal pricey.

People had been trying to fix this problem for a long time. In 1767 and again around 1815 there were plans for a canal, a man-made waterway on which horses could tow heavy barges. Canals were the great transport invention of the 1700s, and a single horse could pull a barge carrying many tons of cargo. But canals are hard to build through hilly country, because water must be kept level, so they need locks, the gated steps that lift boats up and down. The canal plans kept running out of money or support.

A new idea started to win people over: a railway. Horses could pull loaded wagons along a smooth iron track almost as efficiently as along a canal, and a track could climb hills that a canal could not. The engineer George Overton, who had built horse tramroads in South Wales, surveyed a route and recommended one.

The man who did more than anyone to make it happen was Edward Pease of Darlington. Born in 1767, Pease ran a family woollen business and was a member of the Religious Society of Friends, usually called Quakers. Quakers were known for plain clothes, plain speaking, honesty in business and a strong sense of duty. Many Quaker families in Darlington were bankers and merchants who trusted one another and invested together. At a public meeting in Darlington on 13 November 1818, Pease spoke up for the railway and promised investors a five per cent return on their money. He put in £7,000 of his own money, a very large sum then, and so many Quaker families followed him that the line became known as 'the Quaker line'.

sections.heading: Parliament Says Yes, Stephenson Steps In
paragraphs: In Britain, you could not build a long railway across other people's land just because you wanted to. You needed an Act of Parliament, a special law giving a company the right to buy the land it needed, even from owners who did not want to sell. Getting an Act meant months of argument in London, expensive lawyers and plenty of opponents.

The first attempt, in 1819, failed. Some powerful landowners did not want a railway across their estates (one nobleman, the story goes, was mainly worried about his fox-hunting grounds), and the bill was defeated by just 13 votes. The promoters changed the route to avoid the angriest landowners and tried again. This time there was no serious opposition, and the Stockton and Darlington Railway Act received royal assent, the monarch's formal approval, on 19 April 1821.

What the Act said is surprising. It treated the railway rather like a toll road. Anyone with suitable wagons could use the track, as long as they paid a toll, a fee charged per ton of goods per mile. That is why we call it a public railway: it was open to all, not just to one mine owner's wagons. And the Act did not mention steam locomotives at all. The planners imagined horses doing the pulling, as they had done for two hundred years.

There is a well-known story that on the very day the Act was passed, George Stephenson and his friend Nicholas Wood, a mining engineer from Killingworth, walked to Darlington to meet Pease at his home and offer their help. The details may have grown in the retelling over the years, but it is certain that Pease met Stephenson around this time and was deeply impressed by this plain-spoken engine-wright from the Tyne. Stephenson was sure that steam locomotives, not horses, were the future, and he invited Pease to come and see his engines for himself.

By July 1821 the company had decided two important things. First, the line would use edge rails, the kind where flanged wheels ride on top of the rail, rather than the L-shaped plates of a plateway. Second, George Stephenson would resurvey the route. A survey means walking every yard of the land with measuring chains and instruments, working out the heights of hills and valleys, and planning where to dig and where to build up so that the track stays as level as possible. Stephenson's 18-year-old son Robert worked alongside him, carrying instruments, taking measurements and doing calculations.

On 22 January 1822 the shareholders officially made George Stephenson the railway's Engineer, at a salary of £660 a year, a handsome income for a man who had once picked stones out of coal for pennies. Overton played no further part. A few months later, on 23 May 1822, there was a ceremony at St John's Well in Stockton, where the first rail of the line was laid.

In the summer of 1822 Edward Pease travelled north to Killingworth to see Stephenson's locomotives at work for himself. He came away convinced. Stephenson argued strongly for steam, and the company went back to Parliament. A new Act, which received royal assent on 23 May 1823, approved some changes Stephenson had made to the route and, importantly, allowed the company to use 'loco-motives or moveable engines'. For the first time, a public railway had legal permission to run steam locomotives.

Stephenson made another brave choice about the rails, which you met at the end of Part 5. He recommended John Birkinshaw's tough, rolled wrought-iron rails, even though he owned a share in a patent for cast-iron rails. In the end both kinds were used: most of the line was laid with wrought-iron rails weighing 28 pounds per yard, while about 4 miles, mostly at junctions where the shapes were complicated, used heavier cast-iron rails.

sections.heading: The Width That Conquered the World
paragraphs: One of Stephenson's decisions on the Stockton and Darlington would echo around the planet for the next two hundred years: the gauge, the distance between the inner edges of the two rails.

Stephenson did not sit down and calculate a perfect width. He simply used what he knew. The colliery wagonways of north-east England, including his own Killingworth line and the Hetton railway, were laid about 4 feet 8 inches apart, to fit the coal wagons, called chaldron wagons, that the mines already used by the thousand. Building to the same gauge meant those wagons and the skills of the men who worked them could fit straight onto the new line. So the Stockton and Darlington opened with a gauge of 4 ft 8 in (about 1,422 mm).

Soon afterwards, on his next big railway, the Liverpool and Manchester, Stephenson added an extra half inch, making 4 ft 8½ in (1,435 mm). The extra space gave the wheels a little more freedom to move sideways, so they were less likely to bind and jam on curves. The Stockton and Darlington eventually changed to the new measurement too. Because Stephenson and his pupils built so many of Britain's early railways, his gauge spread everywhere. When Parliament settled a fierce battle between gauges in 1846, a story you will hear in Part 8, it chose 4 ft 8½ in as the law for new passenger lines in Great Britain. Today it is called standard gauge, and it is used by about half or more of all the world's railways, from Britain to China and North America.

You may have heard a popular story that the standard gauge comes from the width of Roman chariots, so that a modern train is somehow measured by the backsides of two Roman horses. It is a fun tale, but it is a myth. The real chain is much shorter and simpler. Stephenson took the gauge from the north-east colliery wagonways he worked on. Those wagonways had grown up to suit carts that a horse could pull between its shafts, and wheeled carts in many times and places ended up roughly that width because of the size of a horse, not because anybody copied Roman ruts.

sections.heading: Building a Railway from Scratch
paragraphs: The main line ran about 25 to 26 miles (roughly 40 km) from the collieries near Witton Park and Etherley in the west, past Shildon and Darlington, to the quay at Stockton, with short branch lines to places like Darlington town and Yarm. It was a single track, but with four passing places, called loops, in every mile, so that wagons going in opposite directions could get past each other.

Look closely at the track and you would notice something odd. There were no long wooden sleepers running across from rail to rail as there are today. Each rail sat on its own separate square block, so that horses could walk down the middle of the track without tripping. West of Darlington the blocks were made of stone; to the east, they were oak. The builders were clearly still expecting plenty of horses.

The western end of the line crossed two big hills, and here Stephenson used the trick he had used at Hetton. At the top of each hill, at Etherley and at Brusselton, stood a stationary steam engine, a fixed engine in an engine house. A long rope wound around a huge drum hauled the wagons up one side of the hill, and then they were lowered carefully down the other side. Locomotives worked only on the flatter sections further east.

Rivers needed bridges. Over the little River Gaunless, Stephenson designed one of the earliest iron railway bridges. At Darlington, the architect Ignatius Bonomi designed a handsome stone bridge over the River Skerne. The Skerne Bridge still carries trains today and is thought to be the oldest railway bridge in the world that has been in continuous use. A picture of it even appeared on the back of Bank of England £5 notes from 1990 to 2002.

Building all this cost far more than anyone had estimated, which is a habit railway projects have kept ever since. By September 1825, just before opening, the company had borrowed £60,000 in short-term loans to keep going, and the following year Edward Pease had to lend money twice so that the workers could be paid.

sections.heading: The World's First Locomotive Factory
paragraphs: If the railway was going to use locomotives, someone had to build them. Until now, locomotives had been one-off machines, made by colliery blacksmiths or general engineering workshops in between other jobs. In 1823, George Stephenson, his son Robert, Edward Pease and another Quaker, Thomas Richardson, set up a new firm in Forth Street, Newcastle upon Tyne. They called it Robert Stephenson and Company, after the 19-year-old son, and it was the first company in the world set up specifically to build railway engines. Putting Robert's name on the door was a sign of how much faith his father had in him.

Then, in June 1824, Robert sailed away. He took a three-year job running mines for a British mining company in Colombia, in South America. Historians still wonder whether he wanted adventure, wanted to step out of his famous father's shadow, or both. While he was away, others managed the works, including for a time Timothy Hackworth, the brilliant mechanic from Wylam. On his way home in 1827, waiting for a ship in Cartagena, Robert met a ragged, penniless traveller who turned out to be Richard Trevithick, the pioneer of Part 4. Robert gave him £50 to help pay for his voyage home. The man who built the first railway locomotive was rescued by the son of the man who would make railways famous.

The first engine to roll out of Forth Street for the Stockton and Darlington was originally to be named Active, but it became famous as Locomotion, later called Locomotion No. 1. It was a 0-4-0, meaning it had no small front wheels, four driving wheels, each about 4 feet across, and no small rear wheels. It weighed about 6.5 tons and could reach about 15 mph. Its boiler had just one big flue, a single wide tube carrying the fire's heat through the water, which was a weakness, since it could not make steam very quickly. But it had one important new feature: it is believed to be the first locomotive to use coupling rods, the long bars on the outside that link the driving wheels together so they all turn at once. Coupling the wheels made it much less likely to slip. Locomotion left the works on 16 September 1825, just eleven days before the line was due to open.

sections.heading: Opening Day: 27 September 1825
paragraphs: Imagine the scene early on Tuesday 27 September 1825, near the bottom of Brusselton bank. Huge crowds have walked in from the countryside, some having set off in darkness. Men on horseback trot alongside the track. A train of wagons loaded with coal and a wagon full of sacks of flour has been hauled over the hills, partly by horses and partly by the stationary engine at Brusselton. Now, at Shildon, the star joins it: Locomotion, hissing and puffing, with George Stephenson himself at the controls.

Behind Locomotion came a long, extraordinary train. There were the coal wagons. There was a single passenger carriage, a boxy coach named Experiment, for the company's directors and important guests. And there were 21 brand-new coal wagons that had been fitted with simple seats for the public. The directors had planned room for about 300 passengers. Instead, people clambered on wherever they could, even sitting on top of the coal, and somewhere between 450 and 600 people rode. According to accounts of the day, a man on horseback carrying a flag rode in front of the engine at the start, to warn people out of the way.

The train set off towards Darlington. On a downhill stretch it reached perhaps 10 to 12 mph, faster than most passengers had ever travelled in their lives. Not everything went smoothly. One wagon lost a wheel and had to be left behind, and the train stopped for about 35 minutes while the locomotive was repaired. Still, about 10,000 people were waiting to cheer when it arrived at Darlington. The 8½ miles from Shildon had taken about two hours, including the stops. Six wagons of coal were handed out free to the poor of the town.

After a pause, the train set off again at about half past twelve for Stockton, now made up of 31 vehicles carrying around 550 people, with music and cheering along the way. Along the flat ground east of Darlington the heavily loaded train was slow, but near Stockton, where the track ran beside a road, it picked up speed to about 15 mph. It arrived at Stockton 3 hours and 7 minutes after leaving Darlington, greeted by more crowds and celebrations. That evening, 102 guests sat down to a grand celebration dinner in Stockton Town Hall.

The day was not perfect for everyone. One man was badly hurt when his foot was crushed between vehicles. And according to some accounts, the Pease family stayed away from the celebrations because they were in mourning after a death in the family. If so, the man who had done most to create the railway spent its greatest day in mourning.

sections.heading: How the Line Really Worked
paragraphs: It would be easy to imagine that after opening day, steam trains ran up and down the Stockton and Darlington just as they do on railways today. The reality was much messier, and much more interesting.

Remember that the line was a toll road for wagons. In its early years it was a mix of three kinds of power. Stationary engines hauled wagons over the hills at Etherley and Brusselton. Steam locomotives pulled some coal trains on the flatter parts. And horses, lots of horses, did much of the rest, pulling wagons owned by the company and by independent carriers who simply paid their tolls. The company even introduced a clever invention called the dandy wagon in 1828: a little cart hitched behind the coal wagons, in which the horse could ride downhill while gravity did the work, munching its hay. From late 1828 dandy wagons were compulsory, and people said the horses soon learned to jump in by themselves.

Passengers mostly travelled by horse, not steam. Regular passenger service began on 10 October 1825, with the coach Experiment pulled along the rails by a horse between Stockton and Darlington, at a fare of one shilling. Soon local innkeepers and businessmen were running their own coaches on the line, a little like stagecoaches on rails, cutting the journey to about 1 hour 15 minutes. Between July 1826 and June 1827, somewhere between 30,000 and 40,000 passengers rode the line. Regular steam-hauled passenger trains on the Stockton and Darlington did not arrive until the 1830s.

The locomotives themselves struggled at first. Locomotion broke a wheel soon after the opening and was not back at work until mid-October. A second engine, Hope, arrived in November 1825, and two more similar engines followed in 1826. They often broke down, and some of the directors began to wonder whether horses would have been cheaper after all. Then, in 1828, two boilers exploded, killing both drivers, after safety valves had been fixed down. One of them was Locomotion itself, whose boiler burst on 1 July 1828 at Aycliffe Lane, killing its driver, John Cree.

The person who rescued steam on the line was Timothy Hackworth, who became its locomotive superintendent in 1825 and lived at Shildon. In 1827 he built a much more powerful engine named Royal George, with six coupled wheels and an improved blastpipe that sent the exhaust steam straight up the chimney to make the fire roar. Royal George could haul far heavier trains than the earlier engines, and it helped prove that locomotives were worth it. In 1828 the company reported that steam was saving it about 30 per cent compared with horses.

Most important of all, the railway did what Pease had promised: it made coal cheaper. In the months after opening, the line carried about 10,000 tons of coal. The price of coal in Stockton fell from about 18 shillings a ton to 12 shillings, and by early 1827 to about 8 shillings and sixpence. Ordinary families could afford to heat their homes better, and factories could run their engines more cheaply. Coal shipped from Stockton rose from about 18,500 tons in the year to June 1827 to more than 52,000 tons the next year.

sections.heading: A Town Born from a Railway
paragraphs: Success brought growing pains. The quay at Stockton was too far up the twisting River Tees for big ships. So the company planned an extension further downstream, to a spot where there were just a few farm buildings, called Middlesbrough. The line opened on 27 December 1830, crossing the Tees on a suspension bridge. The bridge turned out to be too weak, its cast-iron plates splitting during a test, so trains had to cross in small groups of four wagons linked by chains. Hackworth's engine Globe hauled the first passengers across to new coal-loading staiths at a place called Port Darlington.

What happened next was astonishing. Before the railway, Middlesbrough had only a handful of houses. A year after the extension opened, more than 2,000 people lived there. Within a few decades it was a large industrial town making iron and steel. It was one of the first towns in the world created by a railway, and many more would follow.

So what was the Stockton and Darlington's place in history? It was not the first railway; wagonways were two hundred years old. It was not the first to carry fare-paying passengers; the Swansea and Mumbles had done that, with horses, since 1807. It was not the first to use steam locomotives in daily work; the Middleton Railway had done that since 1812, and Hetton had run without horses since 1822. What made it special was the combination. It was the first public railway, open to anyone and approved by Parliament, to use steam locomotives. It also showed businessmen everywhere that a railway could be a profitable investment, and it trained a whole generation of engineers and drivers. In 2025, its 200th anniversary was celebrated across north-east England, and a working replica of Locomotion made a journey to Stockton to mark the occasion. The original Locomotion is preserved too, and in recent years it has been shown at museums in both Shildon and Darlington.

News of the line travelled fast. More than 100 miles away, on the other side of England, two great cities were watching closely. Liverpool was a booming port, full of ships bringing raw cotton from America. Manchester, about 35 miles inland, was full of mills spinning that cotton into cloth. Moving goods between them by canal was slow, and the canal owners charged high fees. Merchants in Liverpool and Manchester decided to build a railway of their own, bigger and bolder than anything before it, and they hired George Stephenson to build it. But a hard question remained. Should their trains be pulled by locomotives, or by stationary engines and ropes? To decide which engine was best, they would hold a contest.

deepDive: Historians argue about how to label the Stockton and Darlington Railway, because almost every 'first' attached to it needs a qualifier. It was neither the first railway, nor the first passenger railway, nor the first to use locomotives, nor even the first designed to run without horses (Hetton, 1822). Its claim is the first public railway, built under an Act of Parliament and open to all users on payment of tolls, to use steam locomotives. Its business model was closer to a canal or turnpike than to a modern railway: the company owned the track and charged tolls capped by the 1821 Act at fractions of a penny per ton-mile, while private carriers ran their own horse-drawn wagons and coaches. That mixed traffic caused constant friction, because slow horse trains and faster locomotive trains shared a single line with passing loops and no signals, and it took until the 1830s for the company to take full control of operations. The economics are telling. The line's original purpose was to cut the cost of moving coal from the south-west Durham field to the Tees, and coal prices at Stockton fell by more than half in about eighteen months. Locomotives were not obviously better at first. Early engines like Locomotion had single-flue boilers with small heating surfaces and frequently ran short of steam, and two fatal boiler explosions in 1828 resulted from fixed-down safety valves. Hackworth's Royal George, with six coupled wheels and an effective blastpipe, shifted the balance, and the company's reported saving of about 30 per cent over horse haulage in 1828 suggests that by then steam was cheaper per ton-mile. Some later writers, including Hackworth's son, claimed the directors kept locomotives mainly because Pease and Richardson owned shares in the Stephenson works; the historians Tomlinson and Rolt considered this unfounded, pointing to evidence of genuine cost savings. The gauge story matters too. The line opened at 4 ft 8 in, inherited from local chaldron wagons, and the half inch was added on the Liverpool and Manchester to give extra play on curves. Network effects then did the rest: once enough track and rolling stock existed at one gauge, switching became too expensive, a classic case of an early technical choice being 'locked in' for centuries.
funFact: The Skerne Bridge in Darlington carried the very first Stockton and Darlington train in 1825 and still carries trains today, making it probably the oldest railway bridge in continuous use in the world.

check.q: On the early Stockton and Darlington Railway, how did most passengers travel?
check.a: In coaches pulled along the rails by horses
wrong: In steam-hauled express trains with sleeping cars
In electric trams powered by overhead wires
In carriages pulled by ropes from a canal boat
